observation_summary: Calling addDays(0) or other similar add methods on a MutableDateTime object during a DST transition causes the time to change unexpectedly, even though adding zero should be a no-op.
hypothesis: The implementation of the add methods (addDays, addYears, etc.) in MutableDateTime performs a calculation using the chronology even when the input amount is zero. During DST transitions, this calculation can result in a different time representation due to how the underlying field handles the transition, even if the duration added is zero.
prediction: Adding a guard clause 'if (amount != 0)' to these methods will prevent the unnecessary calculation and preserve the original state when the input is zero.
experiment_rationale: The fix diff shows that every 'add' method in MutableDateTime was updated to include an 'if (amount != 0)' check before calling 'setMillis'. This confirms that the root cause was the lack of a guard to skip the calculation when no change was requested.
reasoning_summary: The bug is caused by the absence of a validation check (a guard) that prevents the execution of a state-changing calculation when the input parameter is zero. Since the fix is to add this missing conditional check, it is classified as 'Checking'.
evidence_used: The fix_diff_oracle shows that every 'add' method (addDays, addYears, etc.) was modified to wrap the 'setMillis' call in an 'if (amount != 0)' block.
The bug report states that addDays(0) changes the value of the object during a DST transition, which is incorrect behavior for a zero-add operation.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the calculation itself is technically involved, the root cause is the failure to skip the calculation when it is unnecessary (i.e., when the input is zero). The fix is a guard, not a rewrite of the calculation logic.
